CancerDojo

By: Michael Duffett | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

Summary:
This is a story of anger survivor who beat the odds, having recovered from life threatening cancer - and he puts it down to using creativity and humour. Conns Berths is one of SA’s top creative thinkers and has run many ad agencies. he was struck down with cancer but decided to fight it through creative thinking.

When he was diagnosed with a severe and extremely rare form of brain cancer in 2006, Bertish immediately set in motion the biggest creative project of his life. He began the process of using his imagination to immerse himself in his bout with cancer. He went straight to the first things he always relied on – his pen, paper and playful, problem-solving attitude. He began toying with cancer, studying the ill people around him, creating visual representations of what he was going through and documenting his experiences through conceptual thinking and storytelling.

He used his imagination to create a drawn series of pen-on-paper metaphors that helped him to visualise his tumour and treatments with intent. Bertish was able to imagine the effects that different treatments would have on the tumour cells. He was also able to concentrate energy where his body needed it most - augmenting the effects of his chemotherapy, radiation and multiple surgeries by linking his mind to his body in a playful targeted way.


Now he is taking his story to the world and already he has even invited at attend overseas companions. he is building a fascinating app, called the Dogo app to encourage cancer sufferers and to provide them with the tools he used.

To be interviewed: Him

and a doctor who will talk on neural imaging which combines positivism and illness.

Press Release:


Cancer Creatively
When Conn Bertish—one of South Africa’s top creative thinkers—was diagnosed with an extremely rare form of brain cancer in 2006 he immediately set in motion the biggest artistic project of his life. He immersed himself in his cancer through comic visuals conjured in his imagination and using his playful, problem-solving attitude. Carte Blanche finds out how Conn’s approach contributed to beating his cancer and debunking fears around this illness.



Script:


Hospital staff must have been taken aback when they wheeled their patient into theatre.

Conn: I was literally lying on the little palette being pushed by these guys going "goooooing, goooooing" which was the sound I imagined that this bouncy brain was making
John: Yeah they must have thought you were a little crazy.
Conn: They did

But far from crazy, Conn Bertish, conceptual artists and one of South Africa’s top creative directors, has discovered his calling in tackling the way we view and deal with cancer. An approach so unique, it has seen him invited to speak at a top international oncology conference.

Sound Up Conn: I wasn’t getting stuck into the funk of cancer, falling into a depression, I was in.

And his mission? To create a mobile platform aimed at debunking the fear surrounding the dreaded disease, which encourages humor and creativity.

LINK: It’s an unusual response to shock but tapping into a seemingly endless well of creative energy is precisely how conn confronted news that most people would dread every hearing, that he had been diagnosed with cancer.

Conn first became concerned back in 2005 when one day he found himself tripping on flat ground and experiencing headaches

Conn: It was literally like somebody jabbing me in the back of my neck with a knife

But when he found that he could not write properly, he knew that he was in deep trouble.

Conn: I think one of the scariest moments of my life

His worst fears were confirmed. An MRI revealed a huge malignant tumor called a medulloblastoma. Before surgery Conn had to sign a consent form accepting that he may lose his sight, hearing or even his life.

Conn: I decided okay I’m not going to lose these senses because I’m going to prepare my brain to be this flexible thing. This bouncy brain.
John: And is that when this process started? Is that when you first started toying with the notion of coming up with this playful way, this creative way of dealing with this?
Conn: Exactly that then became my diet of trying to augment the effects, the efficacy of the treatments that I was undergoing.

His approach may seem a bit off beat but he was tapping into a science called psychoneuroimmunology - for example a positive mindset can boost our bodies immune system.

John: Doctor how important is having a positive attitude?
Dr Davidson: Its critical. It's absolutely critical. A positive patient and a positive family are going to first of all survive the rigors of their treatment more easily and I’m pretty sure they are also going to have a better chance of doing well in the long term.

LINK: After surgery conn returned to work as his ad agencies creative director. He poured his energies into finding creative ways to visualize what was happening inside of his body.

Especially since he still had to endure the rigors of grueling chemotherapy and radiation.

Conn: I was imagining these crazy things. I was imagining that the radiation, that my tumors, my cancer cells were like eggs in a frying pan and then they burned down, suddenly burst into flames burned down and then there was a little pile of ash and then I would blow the pile of ash away...
Jim: The creative energy that poured forth in the months, even during the most difficult times of his treatment, were infectious and contagious.

Conn though had an idea brewing - a social media platform to offer hope to cancer sufferers, providing techniques, which he feels, helped him beat cancer.

Conn: I had actually started calling it my second tumor because it was there and I knew it was powerful and I knew I wanted to get it out.

He roped in colleagues to help bring is idea to life.

Mpumelelo: That’s the ambition that we all have to see this thing take off and become a global phenomenon. I mean it definitely has the potential to be. So it would be great for this to happen.

Last year Conn took a huge gamble and resigned his full time job to concentrate on this project. He started developing an app called the cancer dojo, which would enable cancer patients to participate creatively in their treatment. There will be a host of audio and visual content to tap into. The platform will also provide cancer patients a space to emotionally support each other.

Conn: The app will really be a way in which people facing disease like cancer can literally have a tool with them wherever they go to help them start engaging in their own cancer, in their own way. What I am trying to do with cancerdojo is give people purpose within their disease and if you have that purpose, your immune system is stronger, you are a far more resilient, happier, harder to kill.
Prof Davidson: No one should or could suggest that step away from conventional treatments but there is no question that complementary therapies of all kinds can be helpful.


Professor Alan Davidson, seen here addressing colleagues at an international pediatric oncology conference in Cape Town last year, was so impressed with Conn that when the minister of health had to cancel his opening address, he asked Conn to do the honors.

Sound Up Conn: Happy people are harder to kill, they just are...Its the great Dr. Victor Frankel
Conn: It was amazing. The response was incredible. I came off the podium and was inundated with cards from all around the world of practioners saying how can you help us make this process more user friendly. How can we humanize the treatments? How can we make this process more human?

Another way that conn is hoping to do that is by working with Google to alleviate the fear around cancer.

Conn: So Google search for common cancers, I am going to try and effect and get to the top of the fold so that the first thing somebody sees is not something negative but something that is uplifting and starts assisting them in the first step in engaging and participating in their won healing.

And with the help of Mpumelelo conn is ensuring that the cancerdojo content will reach all South Africans

Mpumelelo: Where I stepped in was to try and take those same lines and that same sentiment and translate it into Xhosa and other languages that kind of weren’t English so that we could kind of spread the message to a broader audience inside the country.

The app and its content are not limited to only those who are creative.

Jim: Some of the simple ways that he is empowering and encouraging people and some of the tools that he has shown to me and we've worked on together are undoubtedly, would support the so called non creative people in tapping into and taking an active role in their disease.
Conn: Anyone can be a creative person. And a lot of people watching will go "ooooh no I cant" but everybody can. There is no right way t creativity. It’s to be curious; it’s about expressing yourself and its not worrying about the outcome or what it looks like?
John: You don’t have to be a Picasso do you, cause as you say your cancer cells could be little stick men with horns. It doesn’t have to be award-winning stuff?
Conn: No, no and again when it comes to pure expression there is no right or wrong.

Conn is seeking local and international partners to complete the app, which is still currently under construction. He hopes it will be released next year.

Conn: I like to say to people who are diagnosed with cancer is that this is the best time in human history to be diagnosed with cancer, it really is. Because we now know so much more about how the mind and the body and the different treatments affect you in a positive way.

And that is the message that Conn is hoping to spread through his cancerdjojo. His ultimate aim is to increase the global cancer survival rate.
